added_claims.speaker: Yo Kit
added_claims.quote: the US market stayed fairly liquid
added_claims.claim: In the April 2025 shock US futures liquidity held up, but emerging-market spreads were all over the place and markets such as South Africa (also hit by local news) were very hard to trade, so execution costs rose most outside the deep markets.
added_claims.testable: yes - bid-offer and slippage data by market

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: there's a lot of divergence uh within the signals that we get as trend followers right now compared to what we normally see uh and certainly also between the long end and the short end
added_claims.claim: During the April 2025 bond rout trend signals within developed-market fixed income diverged unusually, especially between the long and the short end of the curve, so one rates position per country would not capture the moves.
added_claims.indicator: trend signals by maturity within fixed income
added_claims.direction: long end and short end trend in different directions
added_claims.testable: yes - signal dispersion across the curve

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: I would expect that managers who are normally fairly highly correlated um will have seen very different results in the last uh few weeks
added_claims.claim: Niels expected that, because of the speed of the April 2025 move and the sectors involved, normally highly correlated trend followers would show very different results; Yo Kit later cites CFM data that dispersion was not unusual.
added_claims.conditions: fast V-shaped shock; differences in speed and sector mix
added_claims.testable: yes - cross-section of manager returns in April 2025

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: down 5.53 for the month so far as of Tuesday down almost 8% for the year
added_claims.claim: Mid-April 2025 year-to-date: SG CTA almost -8%, SG Trend about -10% and BTop50 about -4.5%, while the short-term traders index was only -0.71%, MSCI World -6.5%, S&P 500 total return -6.9% and the US aggregate bond index +1.6%, so CTAs were losing more than equities in the sell-off.
added_claims.indicator: BTop50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders, MSCI World, S&P 500 TR

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: this is truly a uh something we have not seen in our historical data and whatever back test you did you probably would never have seen uh anything like this uh showing up
added_claims.claim: The April 2025 tariff shock lies outside historical data, so it is a genuine out-of-sample stress test; Niels proposes testing whether CTAs trading 400-600 markets did better or worse than those with a more concentrated portfolio.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare managers by number of markets traded in April 2025

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: whether you are more a continuous system or whether you're more like a breakout type system
added_claims.claim: Reaction speed in a sharp reversal depends not only on lookback parameters but also on model type, for example continuous trend-sizing systems versus breakout-type systems.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare model families in April 2025

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: we can't be sure that it's the CTAs necessarily, right?
added_claims.claim: The extra volatility seen when a trend is extended cannot be attributed to CTAs alone: closet trend followers, macro traders and ordinary de-risking investors also exit at the same time, so it measures the combined impact of trend-following behaviour (Yo Kit accepts this).
added_claims.indicator: unexpected volatility when trend is extended
added_claims.conditions: extended trends followed by a vol spike
added_claims.testable: partly - identification of the CTA share is hard

added_claims.speaker: Yo Kit
added_claims.quote: Well, if I've talked to one, I've talked them all. They're all the same
added_claims.claim: Because CTAs are about 70% loaded on the SG CTA index and about 50% correlated to each other, investors who are used to diversifying across macro managers see CTAs as interchangeable, which hurts the case for allocating to several of them.

added_claims.speaker: Yo Kit
added_claims.quote: if you do breakout you put on the position and you stay in it
added_claims.claim: The cost-aware 'pull back to zero' logic applies to moving-average type predictors, which need fresh price support to hold a strong signal; a breakout system simply puts on the position and stays in it, so it does not manage cost this way.
added_claims.testable: yes - cost analysis by predictor type

added_claims.speaker: Neils Castro Larsson
added_claims.quote: yeah well good until the day it's not
added_claims.claim: Niels warns that skipping a trade because a spiking short-term signal 'will come back' risks missing the trend that does not revert (a type I versus type II error); Yo Kit replies that it is a cost-versus-alpha balance based on mean reversion of the predictor, not a price forecast.
added_claims.testable: yes - backtest cost-gated versus ungated signals

corrections.issue: Mixed speakers: Niels explains that price moves have not lasted long enough for long-lookback models to go short; the point that signal strength was many standard deviations bullish going into February (after an all-time high) is Yo Kit's reply.
corrections.fix: Niels: long-lookback models were not yet short equities in April because the price decline had not lasted long enough (trend following depends on time as well as price). Yo Kit: signals were many standard deviations bullish going into February after the all-time high, so most CTA money was still long equities.

completeness_estimate: 0.88 - the first reader caught the bond-market, first/second-responder, diversification-factor, correlation, cost and mean-reversion arguments; missed the EM liquidity and curve-divergence observations, Niels' dispersion expectation, the mid-April YTD numbers, the out-of-sample stress-test idea, model-type speed, the caveat on attributing vol surprises to CTAs, the 'all the same' allocator problem, the breakout exception to the cost logic and Niels' pushback on cost-gating.
